section_1.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Vectors as Arrows
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed quantities in 2D space. Explain that we can scale them (scalar multiplication) and connect them head-to-tail (vector addition).
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Robot Arm' in 2D: Two segments that can stretch and rotate to reach any point.

section_2.title: Linear Combinations and Span
section_2.content: Define a linear combination as adding scaled vectors (c1v1 + c2v2). Define 'Span' as the collection of all possible points reachable through these combinations. Use a grid animation to show how two non-parallel vectors sweep across the 2D plane.
section_2.example: If a squirrel can jump in vector v1 and vector v2, the 'Span' is the entire territory the squirrel can reach in the park.

section_3.title: Linear Dependence: The Redundant Vector
section_3.content: Explain linear dependence as the existence of 'redundancy'. If one vector lies on the line of another, it adds no new reach. Visually show a vector shrinking to zero or overlapping, indicating it can be 'represented' by others.
section_3.example: Three delivery drones where one drone's path is just the sum of the other two; the third drone is 'linearly dependent' and unnecessary for the mission.

section_4.title: The Concept of a Basis
section_4.content: Define a Basis as the 'minimalist' set: vectors that span the space without any redundancy (linearly independent). Explain that every vector in the space can be represented by a unique set of coordinates using the basis.
section_4.example: A GPS coordinate system: The unit vectors 'East' and 'North' serve as the basis. Every location on the map is just a unique linear combination of these two.

section_5.title: Summary & Visualization
section_5.content: Recap: Span (reach), Linear Dependence (overlap), and Basis (efficient coordinate system). Show a 3D animation where removing a dependent vector collapses a volume into a plane, demonstrating why bases are essential for defining dimensions.
section_5.example: An architect designing a room: The basis vectors are the corners of the floor; if the vectors aren't independent, the room collapses into a flat line!

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Shift grid to the right for better centering
                x = 2.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
